newsitem.title: USA: U.S. May housing starts continue downward trend.
newsitem.headline: U.S. May housing starts continue downward trend.

text.p: U.S. May housing starts posted their third straight monthly decline, but immediate market reaction was muted as the data still showed the housing sector at healthy levels, analysts said.
"The housing numbers are still at high levels, even though they are coming off a little bit," said Joseph Dziwura, vice president and an economist at Sakura Bank Ltd.

"When you look at all the early indicators of the housing market they are still relatively robust," Dziwura said, noting a solid level of mortgage applications, low inventory and favorable mortgage rates.
Despite the slight decrease in May starts, the data were not indicative of sharp declines in the foreseeable future, Dziwura added.

The Commerce Department reported on Tuesday that housing starts fell by 4.8 percent in May to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.397 million versus a revised rate of 1.468 million in the previous month.

The decline represented the third consecutive monthly drop, which has not happened since the January through March period of 1995. Wall Street economists had forecast May starts at a 1.47 million unit annual rate.

May starts of single-family homes were down 2.5 percent from April, and multiple-unit starts dropped 12.2 percent. Permits in May for single-family units dipped 0.4 percent, while permits for multiple-unit dwellings gained 1.3 percent.
Russell Sheldon, vice president and senior economist at Mellon Bank Corp, said he expected a sharp decline in multi-family units.
"Most of the decline between April and May is related to the multi-family being so strong in April," he said, adding that single-family units appeared to be drifting lower.
Sheldon said the Treasury bond rally in recent weeks should set the housing sector up for reacceleration.
"The expectations of homebuilders that came out on Monday are certainly pointing in that direction," Sheldon added.
Some economists said the flooding in the Midwest that had dampened starts in April may have trickled into May numbers.
"(May) is a tricky period to read because of all of the external distortions introduced by nature," said Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
"The flooding conditions may have overlapped into part of May," Seto said, adding that "may have been restraining activity."
Reaction in the U.S. Treasury market to the data had been muted. The benchmark 30-year Treasury inched up following the data, but profit taking wiped away those slight gains.
At 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, the 30-year Treasury benchmark was off 16/32 at 98-19/32 bid.
